pins.kicker: Phone dies in the cold on a hike?
pins.title: 3 fixes
items: Keep it in an inside pocket, close to your body
Switch on airplane mode between photos
Carry a small power bank, kept warm too
pins.sub: Cold drains a phone battery fast. More cold-weather tips are in our Winter Hiking Guide.

pins.title: Have a backup
pins.sub: Cold can shut a phone down early. Download the offline map before you leave and carry a paper map of the trail too.

pins.title: Free entry Nov 11
pins.sub: Most park roads closed for winter on Nov 1. The road from the North Entrance to Mammoth and Lamar Valley stays open. Check nps.gov first.

pins.title: Free day, icy top
items: The South Rim is open all year
Ice forms near the top of the trails
Turn around earlier: the climb out is the hard part
pins.sub: Entrance fees are waived on Veterans Day. Check nps.gov for who qualifies.

pins.kicker: Think the shortest day is darkest?
pins.title: Sunset comes first
pins.sub: In much of the US the earliest sunset is in early December, about two weeks before the shortest day. Pack a headlamp now.

pins.title: They may not be the trail
items: Tracks can lead anywhere: other hikers get lost too
Look for blazes and trail markers
Check your map or GPS often
Lost? Stop, stay put and call for help
pins.sub: Our short guide covers what to do if you get lost.

pins.title: Let your hips carry it
items: Buckle the hip belt over your hip bones
Snug the shoulder straps, not too tight
Pull the load lifters, then clip the chest strap
pins.sub: Most of the weight should ride on your hips, not your shoulders.

pins.title: Never run the stove inside
pins.sub: A stove in a closed tent can fill it with carbon monoxide or set it on fire. Cook outside, then warm up with a hot drink and your sleeping bag.
